records.name: LowkeyKiwi1099
records.text:
Help please 🙏 
I filed a VA claim for my mental health condition and it got denied. The reason they gave was that there was "no qualifying in-service event" — no complaints, treatment, or diagnosis in my service records.

Here's the problem: that's flat-out wrong.

I requested my C&P exam DBQs, and when I read them, the C&P examiner had directly documented my in-service mental health treatment — a diagnosis and medications from during my service — right there in the exam. So the VA's own examiner found the exact evidence the rater claimed didn't exist. The denial contradicts their own paperwork.

I've got a current diagnosis confirmed, and now I've got proof the in-service treatment is documented. From what I understand, the piece I'm still missing is a nexus opinion tying the two together — so I've got an appointment lined up with a psych provider to get a nexus letter.

My questions for anyone who's been through this:

Have any of you dealt with a denial where the C&P examiner's own DBQ contradicted the rater's decision? How'd you attack it? HLR for the error, or Supplemental with a nexus letter?

Any recommendations on getting a strong nexus letter, or providers who know how to write them for the VA?

Anything you wish you'd known before you appealed?

Not looking for anyone to do it for me, just trying to learn from folks who've fought this fight. Appreciate any wisdom. 🇺🇸

records.name: Josh Rincon
records.text:
Your doctor spent more than a decade in medical school and training. 

The person reviewing and denying the claim often has a few weeks of insurance-company training.

One of them decides what treatment you actually need. The other decides whether the insurance company will pay for it. 

That imbalance is baked into the system, and it is one of the reasons so many people feel the American healthcare setup stops making sense the moment a real bill shows up.

records.name: Dane Jones
records.text:
ENOUGH with pretending this is what “coverage” is supposed to feel like.

You can pay premiums for years.

Follow every rule.

Stay in network.

Get referrals.

Submit paperwork.

Do everything exactly the way the system tells you to.

Then the moment your family actually needs expensive care, suddenly you are introduced to a whole new vocabulary:

Denied.

Not medically necessary.

Prior authorization.

Appeal.

Out of network.

Excluded benefit.

And now, on top of worrying about your child, you are expected to become a part time insurance expert just to figure out why the thing you have been paying for is not paying.

That is the part that makes people furious.

Insurance is supposed to protect you from catastrophic costs.

It should not become another obstacle course you have to survive while already dealing with a medical problem.

And I know every denial has its own contract language, medical criteria, appeals process, and specifics.

But from the patient side, that nuance does not make the experience feel any less insane.

You are already scared.

Already tired.

Already trying to make the right medical decisions.

Then a company you have been sending money to for years tells you the care is not covered.

At some point people are allowed to ask a very basic question:

What exactly have I been paying for?

records.name: Hooman Melamed
records.text:
Have you ever had a necessary surgery denied by your health insurance? Listen to this secret recording. 🛑
Today, I am pulling back the curtain on exactly what happens behind closed doors when your insurance company denies your medical care.
I recently had a "peer-to-peer" review call with a doctor representing Aetna. They denied a life-changing surgery for one of my patients suffering from Bertolotti's Syndrome. During the call, the insurance doctor actually admitted that even if he agrees with the clinical evidence, and even if my patients have excellent outcomes... he is not allowed to go against the insurance company's "policy."
Insurance companies are shackling physicians. They are prioritizing corporate policy over evidence-based medicine and patient suffering. It shouldn't matter if I am talking to an insurance doctor, a nurse, or a medical student—if their only job is to read from a corporate script, the system is broken.
We have to fight back. We need to flood our legislators and demand that doctor-to-doctor clinical evidence matters more than an insurance company's bottom line.
Share this video to expose what is really happening in the American healthcare system. Has your insurance ever denied you necessary care? Let everyone know below. 👇
#HealthcareSystem #InsuranceDenial #Aetna #PatientAdvocacy #PeerToPeerReview #DrMelamed #SpineSurgery #HealthInsurance #MedicalEthics #Whistleblower #ChronicPain

records.name: Josh Rincon
records.text:
UnitedHealth Group reported roughly $5.5 billion in net income last quarter. 

At the same time, a KFF analysis of 2025 data found the company denied about 17% of standard prior-authorization requests in its Medicare Advantage plans — roughly 1 in 6

Patients pay premiums every single month, yet the insurer still decides whether many treatments, tests, or procedures get approved through the prior-authorization process. 

The contrast between the profit number and the denial rate is hard to ignore. 

It captures one of the central frustrations of American healthcare: you pay in, but coverage is never fully guaranteed until someone else signs off.
